technologies.how: __global__, __shared__, __shfl_xor_sync, mma.sync, nvcc compilation, and CUDA driver/runtime API.
technologies.name: CUDA C++ / PTX (NVIDIA Flagship)
technologies.what: NVIDIA parallel computing platform and programming model for GPU-accelerated SIMT/tensor compute.
technologies.when: Use when building custom high-performance GPU kernels, FlashAttention fused operators, or Tensor Core matrix acceleration.
technologies.where: Frontier AI LLM cluster training, FlashAttention-v2/v3 kernels, CUDA streams, and PTX assembly acceleration.
technologies.why: Powering NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper (H100/H200), and Grace-Hopper supercomputers for FlashAttention, TensorRT-LLM, and Megatron-LM.

technologies.how: JIT kernels, block pointers, masks, program IDs, autotuning, and compiler lowering.
technologies.name: Triton
technologies.what: Defines high-throughput GPU kernels with Python syntax and compiler-managed block programming.
technologies.when: Use after profiling shows framework kernels are inadequate and the target GPU is supported.
technologies.where: Fused attention, normalization, quantization, MoE routing, and custom inference operations.
technologies.why: It exposes GPU performance without hand-authoring all CUDA indexing and scheduling details.

technologies.how: Typed functions, structs, ownership, SIMD vectors, and MLIR-based lowering.
technologies.name: Mojo
technologies.what: Combines Python-like authoring with systems-level types, ownership, and accelerator-oriented compilation.
technologies.when: Use when Python ergonomics must reach native or accelerator performance in one language.
technologies.where: AI kernels, SIMD tensor code, model serving components, and MLIR-backed optimization.
technologies.why: Its compiler stack targets heterogeneous AI hardware while retaining familiar syntax.

technologies.how: GraphProto nodes, tensors, opsets, shape inference, metadata, and execution providers.
technologies.name: ONNX
technologies.what: Represents machine-learning computation as a portable typed graph independent of the training framework.
technologies.when: Use when a model must move between frameworks or run across multiple inference backends.
technologies.where: Model exchange, runtime deployment, graph inspection, optimization, and hardware-provider selection.
technologies.why: It separates learned graph semantics from any one training library and enables portable validation.

technologies.how: Operations, regions, SSA values, dialects, rewrite passes, and lowering pipelines.
technologies.name: MLIR
technologies.what: Provides extensible intermediate representations and dialects across abstraction levels.
technologies.when: Use when one operation must be progressively transformed from domain semantics to machine code.
technologies.where: Compiler pipelines, tensor lowering, accelerator backends, DSLs, and hardware-specific optimization.
technologies.why: It makes compiler passes and hardware dialect boundaries explicit and reusable.

technologies.how: Modules, linear memory, imports, exports, instructions, and WASI/capability hosts.
technologies.name: WebAssembly
technologies.what: Provides a portable, capability-constrained bytecode target for sandboxed execution.
technologies.when: Use when untrusted or portable code must run within explicit host capabilities.
technologies.where: Browser modules, plugin systems, edge runtimes, and zero-trust agent tools.
technologies.why: Its validated bytecode and host-controlled imports create a small cross-platform isolation boundary.
